meaning.evidence: Every figure and step survives (9,300 gallons, nine percent, 12,000 gallons, two hours, 10 minutes, five years, 3,000 gallons, 180 showers, 500 gallons, 60 loads). The additions are colour: "Not bad for an arvo's tinkerin', ay?", "or you'll cop a faceful!". "turn the water off at the main" is a slight narrowing of "turn off the water line".

sense.evidence: Terms fit: "dunny flappers", "drippin' taps", "cistern", "rocks up in the bowl", "clapped-out", "the folding stuff", "sing out when your place is usin' water funny".

authenticity.evidence: Mostly a real Australian voice: "Have a geek", "have a yarn to the blokes at your local hardware", "down the hardware". The steady g-dropping ("wastin'", "findin'", "leakin'") and "bleedin'" (more British) lean a little stagey.

register.evidence: A full level-4 retelling of a government fact sheet, with swearing at dad level: "where the bugger's comin' from".

tone.evidence: Keeps the helpful, practical how-to voice under the slang; the warnings stay warnings: "Make sure you flush straight after, mind, or the dye'll stain the tank."

flow.evidence: Reads aloud well, though some sentences sprawl: "Plumber's tape, or teflon tape, you can grab at most hardware shops, it's easy to put on, and it helps keep leaks in check."

variety.evidence: Wide range with nothing leaned on: "geek", "squiz", "clapped-out", "gizmos", "Strewth", "beaut", "cop a faceful", "had it".

essence.evidence: Still clearly the EPA leak guide, with the same sections, stats and tips in order.

problems.quote: Don't forget to turn the water off at the main before you start, or you'll cop a faceful!
problems.original: Tip: Don't forget to turn off the water line before you start!
problems.why: "at the main" narrows the original's instruction (an isolation valve would also do), and the faceful is added colour.

problems.quote: have a yarn to the blokes at your local hardware
problems.original: consult your local hardware store, home improvement, retailer
problems.why: "the blokes" assumes the staff are men; harmless but a narrowing.

A.summary: A full, natural level-4 retelling that keeps every number and instruction and adds only colour. Slightly heavy on g-dropping.

meaning.evidence: Most text is the original verbatim, but a few swaps change it: "tucker colouring" for food colouring, "60 heaps of dishes" for 60 loads, and "Give a stuff about the width" for pay attention to it.

sense.evidence: Several terms take the wrong sense: "tucker colouring" (food dye is not tucker), "60 heaps of dishes", "Give a stuff about the width" (an idiom for caring, mostly in the negative), "water metre" (a length unit, not a gauge), "a beaut seal".

authenticity.evidence: Stock interjections bolted onto untouched American text: "Jeez Louise, these types of leaks are often easy to fix", "Bugger me, to check for leaks", "Anyway, faucet Leaks". US "faucet" is kept throughout.

register.evidence: Far lighter than level 4 in substance: whole paragraphs untouched ("Leak detection and flow monitoring devices can help you identify leaks or alert you to irregular water use"). The interjections add noise, not register.

tone.evidence: The fact-sheet tone survives where untouched, but "Bugger me" and "Jeez Louise" in front of neutral statements make the advice exclamatory for no reason.

flow.evidence: Jarring joins and broken grammar: "Anyway, faucet Leaks" as a heading, "Take a geek at your water usage during a colder month, such as January or February, ay.", "home improvement, retailer, or a licensed plumber, mate."

variety.evidence: Leans on a few tokens: "dunny" over and over, "beaut" twice, plus filler openers ("Mind you", "Well,", "Anyway").

essence.evidence: Recognisably the EPA guide, since most of it is the guide, but the misused terms muddy some instructions.

problems.why: "tucker" means a meal; "tucker colouring" is not a thing an Australian would say for food dye.
"heaps" is not a unit; the dishwasher-load comparison becomes nonsense.

problems.quote: Give a stuff about the width of the flapper
problems.original: Pay attention to the width of the flapper
problems.why: "give a stuff" means care (usually "couldn't give a stuff"); it is crude and wrong for an instruction.
"metre" is the unit of length; the device is spelt "meter" in Australia too.
A filler word stuck onto a section heading breaks the layout, and US "faucet" is left in.

problems.original: To check for leaks in your home
problems.why: A surprise interjection with nothing to be surprised at.

problems.original: These types of leaks are often easy to fix

B.summary: Mostly untranslated, with stock interjections and several word swaps that take the wrong sense or break grammar. Far from the brief.

meaning.evidence: All figures and steps survive faithfully: "If the meter's moved at all, you've probably got a leak", "replace it at least every five years". "are forever causing leaks" mildly overstates "frequently".

sense.evidence: Terms fit: "Suss out toilet leaks", "a once-over", "give you a heads-up about weird water use", "get on the blower to an experienced handyperson", "get stuck in".

authenticity.evidence: Mostly natural Australian: "chew through", "drippy taps", "clapped-out", "get on the blower". "a doddle" (British) and "a bit of coin" (more American) are off-notes.

register.evidence: Clearly Aussie and dad-level clean ("where the bugger's coming from"), but a notch lighter than level 4 in places, where sentences stay close to the source: "Leak detection and flow monitoring gadgets can help you find leaks".

tone.evidence: The practical, encouraging how-to voice is intact: "Don't forget to turn the water off before you get stuck in!"

flow.evidence: Smooth and well joined throughout: "Most of these are a doddle to fix, needing only a few tools and bits of hardware that'll pay for themselves in water savings."

variety.evidence: Good range ("squiz", "suss out", "once-over", "gizmo", "strewth", "on the blower"), but "toilet" and "dunny" alternate a little arbitrarily.

essence.evidence: Plainly the EPA guide, with the same structure and all the content, retold.

problems.why: "doddle" is British; "a piece of piss" is out at this vulgarity, but "a cinch" or "dead easy" would be fine.
"coin" for money is more American slang; "a few bucks" would be more local.

C.summary: Faithful, smooth and natural, a touch lighter than level 4, with a couple of non-Australian slang choices.
